c.tagline: One of Earth's most remote capitals - Georgian streets, 699 steps, Napoleon's exile.

taxi.fareNote: There are no ride-hailing apps; taxis and hired cars are booked by phone or through the Inside St Helena app, and there is a taxi stand on Main Street in Jamestown. Bring cash - there are no ATMs on the island.

emergency.note: 999 reaches police, fire, and ambulance across the island.

hood_desc: The Georgian capital wedged in a narrow valley between two steep cliffs, its single Main Street lined with 18th- and 19th-century buildings, the Castle, St James' Church, the Museum of St Helena, shops, and the base of Jacob's Ladder; the walkable heart of the island and where most visitors stay.

The island's largest settlement, a residential suburb perched at the top of Ladder Hill directly above Jamestown, with shops, homes, and sweeping views over the town and Atlantic; a practical, quieter base a short drive from the center.

A cooler, greener plateau district to the east built around Napoleon's exile: Longwood House, where he lived and died in 1821, and the site of his original tomb both sit here, surrounded by rolling farmland.

A lush rural district in the island's green interior, home to St Paul's Cathedral, Plantation House (the Governor's residence and home of Jonathan the giant tortoise), and gardens; peaceful and scenic.
A quiet residential district on the ridge just east of Jamestown, with homes, gardens, and walking access to the valley and the heart-shaped waterfall viewpoint; calm and local.

water.note: Treated tap water in Jamestown is safe to drink.

transit.hours: Public buses run limited daytime routes (roughly 7:00 AM to early evening, reduced on weekends); taxis run on call.
transit.note: St Helena has a small public bus network linking Jamestown with Half Tree Hollow, Longwood, Levelwood and other districts, supplemented by taxis and hired cars; Jamestown itself is walkable, though the surrounding hills are steep.
transit.pay: Bus and taxi fares are paid in cash (St Helena pounds or GBP); there is no transit card.

food.name: St Helena Tuna Fishcakes
food.desc: The island's national snack: line-caught tuna mashed with potato, onion, chilli and herbs, shaped into patties and fried golden. Eaten in a bread roll.

places.name: Anne's Place
places.note: Long-running garden restaurant famous island-wide for its fishcakes; a fixture of Jamestown lunch since the 1980s.

places.name: St Helena Coffee Shop
places.note: Cooks fishcake rolls to order with fresh tuna; popular quick stop for visitors off the wharf.

places.name: Orange Tree Restaurant
places.note: Kitchen specialising in Saint cooking and seafood; fishcakes are one of its signature plates.

food.name: Saint Helena Plo
food.desc: The island's celebration dish: rice slow-cooked with chicken, beef or pork, onion and spices until rich and savoury. Served at weddings and Sunday lunches.

places.name: Anne's Place
places.note: Best-known place to try plo without a family invitation; often on the daily specials board.

places.name: Consulate Hotel
places.note: Georgian hotel dining room serving Saint classics alongside a general menu; plo appears on rotating specials.

places.name: Mantis St Helena
places.note: Converted barracks hotel restaurant giving island dishes a smarter treatment for visitors.

food.name: Grilled Wahoo or Tuna Steak
food.desc: Thick steaks of wahoo, yellowfin tuna or marlin landed that morning, grilled simply with lemon and served with rice, salad or chips.

places.name: Orange Tree Restaurant
places.note: Wahoo, grouper, marlin and tuna steaks are the house specialities, cut from the day's landings.

places.name: Mantis St Helena
places.note: Hotel restaurant buying direct from the island fishery; the fish of the day changes with the boats.

places.name: Wharf and Jamestown fish landing
places.note: Where the catch comes ashore; the freshest fish on the island passes through here before reaching kitchens.

food.name: Fish 'n' Batter with Bullseye
food.desc: Saint-style battered fish, usually the local bullseye, deep-fried crisp and served with chips. The island's everyday takeaway staple.

places.name: Frankies
places.note: Weekend takeaway van doing battered fish, curries and fishcakes; a Jamestown institution for late trade.

places.name: Philly's Takeaway
places.note: Lunchtime favourite serving fried fish, ribs and fishcakes from the Parade; busy with locals.

places.name: Orange Tree Restaurant
places.note: Does a sit-down version with fried bullseye and grouper alongside its fishcakes.

food.name: Coconut Fingers
food.desc: Sweet fried pastry fingers rolled in coconut, a Saint teatime treat sold at takeaways, fetes and church sales across the island.

places.name: Frankies
places.note: One of the few takeaways reliably making coconut fingers alongside milkshakes and ice cream.

places.name: St Helena Coffee Shop
places.note: Stocks island bakes and sweets to go with its coffee; good place to pick up Saint baking.

places.name: Jamestown Market
places.note: Weekly market where home bakers sell coconut fingers, cakes and preserves.

food.name: Curry and Rice, Saint Style
food.desc: A mild island curry of chicken, beef or fish, sweetened with fruit and thickened with local vegetables, always served over a big plate of rice.

places.name: Anne's Place
places.note: Home-style curries served with rice and veg in the shade of the gardens.

places.name: Frankies
places.note: Weekend curry is a regular on the takeaway board and a local favourite.

places.name: Consulate Hotel
places.note: Reliable full-service option for a sit-down curry lunch in the centre of town.

food.name: St Helena Coffee
food.desc: Green-tipped Bourbon Arabica grown from 1733 Yemeni stock, among the rarest and most expensive coffees in the world. Bright, delicate and low-yield.

places.name: St Helena Coffee Shop
places.note: The easiest place in town to drink island-grown coffee by the cup rather than buy beans.

places.name: Rosemary Gate / island coffee estates
places.note: The plantations where the beans are grown; estate visits and tastings are arranged for visitors.

places.name: Consulate Hotel
places.note: Serves St Helena coffee in its lounge, a comfortable spot to try it slowly.

food.name: Tungi Spirit
food.desc: Clear spirit distilled from tungi, the wild prickly pear that grows across the island's dry slopes. Crisp and faintly fruity, unique to St Helena.

places.name: St Helena Distillery
places.note: The world's most remote distillery and the only maker of Tungi; tours and tastings by arrangement.

places.name: Consulate Hotel bar
places.note: Central bar that pours Tungi neat or long; a straightforward place to try it in town.

places.name: Mantis St Helena bar
places.note: Hotel bar stocking the island's spirits and mixing Tungi into cocktails.

landmarks: Jacob's Ladder
A dizzying 699-step staircase climbing 180 metres from Jamestown to Ladder Hill Fort, Saint Helena's most famous calf-burning challenge.
Longwood House
Napoleon Bonaparte's final residence and museum, where the exiled emperor spent his last years amid period furnishings and windswept gardens.
Napoleon's Tomb (Sane Valley)
A quiet, geranium-ringed grave site in a green valley where Napoleon lay from 1821 until his remains returned to Paris in 1840.
Plantation House and Jonathan the tortoise
The Georgian governor's mansion whose lawns are patrolled by Jonathan, a giant tortoise reckoned the world's oldest living land animal.
High Knoll Fort
A commanding 19th-century hilltop fortress with panoramic views across the island's peaks, pastures and endless South Atlantic.
St. James' Church
The oldest Anglican church in the southern hemisphere, founded in 1774, anchoring Jamestown's remarkably preserved Georgian main street.
The Castle and Castle Gardens
Saint Helena's 17th-century seat of government beside the seafront, with shady gardens that host the island's memorials and birdlife.
Diana's Peak National Park
The island's highest point at 823 metres, a cloud-forest ridge walk through tree ferns and endemic species found nowhere else.
Museum of Saint Helena
A harbourside museum in a restored warehouse recounting the island's saga of explorers, slavery, Boer prisoners and Napoleon.
Heart Shaped Waterfall
A romantic cascade tumbling over a heart-shaped cliff face above Jamestown, reached by a gentle valley walk from town.

train.note: There has never been a railway on Saint Helena. The nearest thing is Jacob's Ladder, the 699-step inclined plane rising out of Jamestown that once carried an ore tramway and is now purely a walking challenge. All movement on the island is by road, and there is obviously no international rail on a mid-Atlantic island.

bus.note: No bus crosses a border - Saint Helena is roughly 1,900 km from the African coast. On the island the Saint Helena Government runs a basic minibus service radiating from the Market in central Jamestown to Half Tree Hollow, Longwood, Levelwood, Sandy Bay and Blue Hill, mostly on weekday-only timetables with a handful of runs each day and little or nothing on Sundays. Fares are paid in cash to the driver and timetables are published by the Saint Helena Government (https://www.sainthelena.gov.sh/). Most visitors hire a car or use the small taxi fleet, since the bus network is designed around islanders' shopping trips rather than sightseeing.

ferry.note: The RMS Saint Helena, the island's scheduled passenger ship from Cape Town, made her final voyage in 2018 after Saint Helena Airport opened, and nothing has replaced her - there is no scheduled passenger ferry today. Freight arrives roughly monthly on a chartered cargo vessel from Cape Town, which is a freight operation rather than a way for travellers to book passage, and cruise ships that call must tender passengers ashore at the Jamestown wharf because there is no deep-water berth. Access is now effectively by air, on Airlink's weekly Saturday service from Johannesburg with a fuel stop at Walvis Bay, plus occasional Cape Town and Ascension Island flights.
